name: PABA

lead: PABA was one of the first chemical sunscreen ingredients, patented in 1943, and was widely used in mid-century suncare to prevent burning and sun-aged skin.

It absorbs UVB (about 290 to 320 nm) and passes most UVA. Its use fell after reports of allergic contact dermatitis, photocontact dermatitis and clothing stains, and early-1980s lab work suggested it could sensitise cells to UV damage. Long-term appearance trials of PABA are not available.

paras: Today it is mostly encountered as history, as the ingredient modern sunscreens moved away from. Water-insoluble derivatives such as padimate O have continued in some cosmetics, and PABA itself also occurs naturally in foods like liver, yeast and whole grains.

Documented risks include allergic contact dermatitis, photocontact dermatitis and eye irritation. The EU banned it as a sunscreen ingredient in 2008, and the US FDA proposed limited allowance in 2019.

angle.text: PABA was one of the first sunscreen actives, used for decades to prevent burning and sun-aged skin. It absorbs UVB light, and less UV damage means less photoaging over time. It is now known mainly as the ingredient modern formulas moved away from.

lead: PABA (para-aminobenzoic acid, 4-aminobenzoic acid) is a small aromatic compound with an amino group and a carboxyl group on opposite sides of a benzene ring. It occurs naturally in foods such as liver, brewer's yeast, mushrooms and whole grains, and is an intermediate in folate synthesis in bacteria, plants and fungi.[1] In appearance culture it is known as one of the first active ingredients used in sunscreens.[1]

As a sunscreen filter, PABA absorbs UVB light (roughly 290 to 320 nm) and lets most UVA pass.[1] It was patented in 1943.[1] Its use declined after reports of allergic contact dermatitis and photocontact dermatitis, staining of clothing, and laboratory studies in the early 1980s suggesting it could sensitise cells to UV damage.[1] The European Union banned it as a sunscreen ingredient in 2008, and in 2019 the US FDA proposed allowing only limited use.[1] Water-insoluble derivatives such as padimate O have continued in some cosmetics.[1]
Evidence for PABA as an appearance product is limited to its historical role as a UVB filter; no current clinical trials of it as a sunscreen appear in the sources reviewed.

paras: Sunscreen: PABA was among the first sunscreen actives and acts by absorbing UVB radiation.[1] Its derivative padimate O remains in some products such as mascara, concealer and matte lipsticks.[1]

Other uses: PABA is a building block for several local anaesthetics (for example butamben and tetracaine) and other drugs.[1] Potassium aminobenzoate has been used for fibrotic skin conditions such as Peyronie's disease, although the evidence is described as weak.[1] PABA has also been used to check the completeness of 24-hour urine collections.[1][2] Supplement sellers promote it for fatigue, skin and hair-colour claims; the Wikipedia article notes that no PABA deficiency syndrome is recognised in humans.[1]

PABA can cause allergic contact dermatitis and photocontact dermatitis, and it is an eye irritant.[1] It is also formed when ester-type local anaesthetics are metabolised, and many reactions attributed to those anaesthetics are described as reactions to PABA.[1] It is considered largely non-toxic by mouth in animal tests.[1]
A 1982 study reported that PABA sensitised mammalian cells to near-UV killing, one of the findings cited in its decline as a sunscreen ingredient.[1]

PABA has the formula C7H7NO2 and a molar mass of about 137 g/mol. Industrially it is made mainly by reducing 4-nitrobenzoic acid.[1] Sulfonamide antibiotics resemble PABA and work by blocking the bacterial enzyme dihydropteroate synthetase.[1] Humans do not use PABA directly to make folate.[1]

PABA was patented in 1943 and became an early standard sunscreen active.[1] A 1975 rodent study reported protection against UV-induced skin tumours.[1] From the early 1980s, in vitro and animal findings raised phototoxicity concerns, and allergy and staining problems accelerated its decline.[1] The EU banned it in 2008.[1]

A homeopathic oral B-vitamin complex product that lists PABA as an ingredient is registered on the US DailyMed database, with a label stating its claims rest on traditional homeopathic practice and are not accepted medical evidence.[3]

No studies found of PABA as an appearance or sunscreen treatment in the sources reviewed. Registered studies involving PABA have examined it as a tracer or biochemical marker, for example a small imaging study of carbon-11-labelled PABA.[4] Laboratory research on UV filters in general, including a 2001 study of six UV screens, has examined hormone-like activity in cell and animal systems.[5]
